Architecture.label: 01 — Architecture
Architecture.title: Engineering, not decoration.
Architecture.intro: Every pixel is a tolerance, every frame a commitment. High-ROI digital ecosystems are built here in two layers: a front end that feels calibrated, not merely quick, and enterprise automation engineered to fail safely.
Architecture.c1Title: Video, not code. Cinema, in the browser.
Architecture.c1Text: We left heavy render engines and stuttering animation layers behind. Your hero and showcase streams are served as native MP4/WebM video, decoded by the device’s own video hardware, so the stream costs the processor little.
Architecture.c1Tags: H.264 · VP9 · Loads on demand · Space reserved, no layout shift
Architecture.c1VideoLabel: A glass monolith turning slowly on a black background
Architecture.c2Text: Scrolling and transitions follow the display’s own frame rhythm. On desktops with a mouse or trackpad, Lenis eases the scroll; touch devices keep their native, immediate scroll. The page moves like an extension of your hand, not under it.
Architecture.c2Tags: Lenis smooth scroll · requestAnimationFrame · GPU-composited transforms
Architecture.c2Caption: Measured while scrolling on a 60 Hz display. {profile}. {date}.
Architecture.c2GraphAlt: A line chart of frame time, flat at the 60 Hz frame interval
Architecture.c3Title: Beauty becomes luxury when it can be measured.
Architecture.c3Text: Performance, accessibility, best practices, SEO: four rings, measured on this very page. A visitor who leaves in three seconds is never won back by a manifesto, so we measure first and say it afterwards.
Architecture.c3Tags: CLS · LCP · TBT · measured, dated and sourced
Architecture.c3Detail: Desktop: CLS {cls}, LCP {lcp}, TBT {tbt}. Mobile (simulated slow 4G, 4× CPU slowdown): performance {mobile}.
Architecture.c4Title: Built for the day something fails.
Architecture.c4Text: At enterprise scale, something always fails. So the automation is built around that fact: redundant queue architectures keep events moving when one path goes quiet, and webhooks are signed and verified before anything trusts them.
Architecture.c4Tags: Redundant queues · Signed webhooks · Idempotent delivery · Bounded retries
Architecture.c5Title: Joined to the systems you already run.
Architecture.c5Text: Salesforce, SAP, HubSpot and Oracle are part of the architecture from the first sketch, so leads, orders and records can move between the site and the systems your business already runs on.
Architecture.c6Title: Nothing is trusted until it is verified.
Architecture.c6Text: Every message that crosses a boundary is signed, verified by the receiver and sealed before it moves on. The steps below run live in your browser, so you can break one and see exactly where the message stops.
Architecture.c6Tags: HMAC-SHA256 · Zero-trust verification · AES-256-GCM · Idempotency keys

Studio.label: 03 — Studio
Studio.title:
Exact by habit.
Silent by default.
Studio.lead: We are a digital architecture studio for owners, partners and principals whose name is the business. We work the way a good architect does: to a drawing, to a tolerance, and under discretion.
Studio.p1Text: A defect is something to design out, not to apologise for. Every change is audited, smoke-tested and checked on the live site before we call it done, and what we publish about performance is measured, dated and sourced. Zero defects is the standard we work to, never a promise we could sign for you.
Studio.p2Text: A mutual NDA can be signed before our first working session. Client work is never shown without written consent, which is why the showcase holds studio specimens only. This site sets no cookies and runs no analytics, and every briefing is read by a person.
Studio.p3Text: Video is decoded by the device’s own video hardware, motion is composited on the GPU, scrolling follows the display’s frame rhythm, and the frame budget is measured. Nothing decorative is allowed to cost a visitor a frame.
Studio.howLead: Three decisions give this site its feel, and each has tolerances. What follows describes what the code on this page actually does.
Studio.n1Title: Hardware-decoded video and a GPU cinema layer
Studio.n1Summary: The motion on this site is video the device decodes in hardware, plus one WebGL layer that backs off the moment it costs a frame.
Studio.n1s1: Each scene is a seamless eight-second loop rendered once at 1920 × 1080 and 30 frames per second, then encoded as H.264 (MP4) with VP9 (WebM) as the fallback. No animation engine is shipped to the browser.
Studio.n1s2: The browser hands the stream to the device’s own video decoder, which on most phones and laptops is dedicated hardware, so the processor stays free for the page.
Studio.n1s3t: Loaded and played only when seen.
Studio.n1s3: A clip is not downloaded until it is about to play. It plays while on screen or under the pointer, pauses when it leaves or the tab is hidden, stays still for visitors who prefer reduced motion or save data, and always has a pause control.
Studio.n1s4t: One WebGL layer, on a budget.
Studio.n1s4: The light behind the page is raw WebGL2 in two passes, scene then finish, asking for the high-performance GPU. It is capped at a pixel ratio of 1.25, runs its ambient state at 30 frames per second and, if the average frame over 90 frames exceeds 24 ms, lowers its resolution step by step before retiring itself and leaving the CSS fallback.
Studio.n1Tolerances: Pixel ratio ≤ 1.25 · scene pass 50 % down to 30 % · retreat above 24 ms (90-frame average) · loops of 8 s at 30 fps
Studio.n2Summary: The page does its work once per frame, and only for what is visible.
Studio.n2s1t: One read, one write per frame.
Studio.n2s1: Scroll handlers only record that something changed. A single requestAnimationFrame callback takes at most one layout measurement and writes the result into CSS custom properties, and only while the section is on screen.
Studio.n2s2: Animation is limited to transform, opacity and clip-path. Width, height, top and left never animate, so a frame is a composite of layers rather than a new layout.
Studio.n2s3: Anything that loops, such as a beam of light, a scroll cue or a video, pauses as soon as it leaves the screen, and everything stops while the tab is hidden.
Studio.n2s4: A scroll through the whole page held a median frame time of {median} and a 99th percentile of {p99} ({profile}, {date}).
Studio.n2Tolerances: One layout read per frame · animated properties: transform, opacity, clip-path · 16.7 ms frame budget at 60 Hz
Studio.n3Summary: Smooth scrolling is a courtesy for the desktop pointer, and it is switched off wherever it could do harm.
Studio.n3s1: It starts only for a mouse-like pointer and never when the visitor prefers reduced motion. Both conditions are watched live, so a hybrid laptop or a changed setting switches it on or off without a reload. Touch devices keep their native scroll and never download the library.
Studio.n3s2: A duration of 1.2 seconds on a cubic-bezier(0.16, 1, 0.3, 1) ease, driven by the library’s own animation-frame loop. Links within the page glide on the same curve and leave room for the fixed header.
Studio.n3s3: It stands still while the entry gate is open, and the briefing and every dialog scroll natively. After a jump, focus and the address end up where a native anchor would leave them.
Studio.n3s4: The library is a separate chunk, requested by a dynamic import only after the page has painted and only when both conditions hold. It is not part of the first load.
Studio.n3Tolerances: Duration 1.2 s · ease cubic-bezier(0.16, 1, 0.3, 1) · header offset 88 px · fine pointer only · off under reduced motion
Studio.manifestoLead: Not slogans: each line is something this page does, and you can check it yourself.
Studio.m1Text: Data, failure modes and tolerances are written down and agreed before any code. A build that cannot be drawn is not started.
Studio.m2Text: We publish numbers with a date, a profile and a source, and say nothing we cannot measure.
Studio.m3Text: When a part is missing, the system refuses and says so. It never answers “received” for a message nobody got.
Studio.m4Text: No cookies, no analytics, a third party only where a bot check is needed. What a client tells us is read by a person, not by a tracker.
Studio.m5Title: Test the claim, not the page.
Studio.m5Text: Security and integration claims are backed by tests we run before every release: signed messages, sealed envelopes, and a reference queue that loses nothing and applies nothing twice in every tested failure.
Studio.f1Text: The enterprise security flow on this page signs and seals a message with your browser’s own Web Crypto: the same primitives, and the same tests, as our reference architecture.
Studio.f2Text: Open your network tab: nothing is stored on your device and nothing loads from a third party, except the Cloudflare bot check on the briefing form.
Studio.f3Text: Every script carries a one-time nonce and the browser blocks the rest. A scan for violations is part of our release checks.
Studio.drawingTitle: The path of your briefing, drawn first.
Studio.drawingLead: The first rule above, applied to the form on this page. Every box is code in our repository, and the figures are the ones in that code.
Studio.drawingAlt: System flow of the briefing form. The browser sends the answers with a Turnstile token to one route, which checks the origin and the rate limit, validates the schema, runs the bot checks, sanitises the text and sets a priority class, then delivers by signed webhook or SMTP over TLS to the studio mailbox. Any failed step refuses the request and offers the visitor an email draft.
Studio.drawingLegend: Solid line: the path of a briefing. Dashed line: any failed step ends there. The request is refused and your answers open as an email draft, so nothing is ever reported as received that was not.
Studio.founding: Founded by an architect who works in the dark and designs for low-tolerance enterprise infrastructures. We do not operate on social praise or public noise. We build, measure, and fail closed.

queue.title: Fail-safe queue simulator
queue.lead: Block the primary channel and watch the events wait safely in the standby queue instead of being lost. Then restore it.
queue.statusIdle: All channels are healthy. Send events to begin.
queue.statusFlowing: Events are flowing over the primary channel.
queue.statusBlocked: The primary channel is blocked. {waiting} events are waiting safely in the standby queue; {delivered} were delivered.
queue.statusDraining: The primary channel is back. The standby queue is draining in order.
queue.statusDone: {delivered} of {accepted} events delivered, in order, once each. Lost: {lost}.
queue.caption: A model of the pattern, not a measurement of a real system. Here nothing is dropped because the standby queue is durable; a real deployment has to be tested on its own.

security.title: Enterprise security flow
security.lead: A signed message, verified and sealed on its way to a business system. Every step is computed live in your browser with Web Crypto and throwaway keys.
security.clientText: The client builds the message and gives it a unique key.
security.signText: A keyed hash is computed over the exact bytes being sent. Change one byte and the signature no longer matches.
security.verifyText: The receiver trusts nothing: it recomputes the signature, checks that the timestamp is fresh and that the key has not been seen before.
security.encryptText: Only a verified message moves on, sealed with AES-256-GCM: confidentiality and tamper detection in one step.
security.deliverText: It reaches the business system, is decrypted there, and the receipt is acknowledged. Salesforce, SAP and Oracle are examples of targets.
security.statusIdle: Ready. Send a message and follow it through the five steps.
security.outDelivered: Delivered. Decrypted at the destination: the plaintext matches the original.
security.outRejected: Rejected at the zero-trust check. The message never reached the business system.
security.outDuplicate: Acknowledged, not processed twice: the idempotency key had already been seen.
security.outUnavailable: Web Crypto is not available in this browser context, so the live computation cannot run.
security.caption: Runs in your browser with throwaway keys; nothing leaves this page. It demonstrates the pattern; it does not describe, measure or certify any production system, and no partnership with the products named is implied. The signing step is the same pattern this site uses to deliver its own briefings.

integration.title: One event, four systems
integration.lead: Choose a system. The same event is mapped into the shape that system expects, and each line shows which field feeds which.
integration.status: Fields mapped: {count}. Record: {object}. The event id travels in {field}, so a retry cannot create a second record.
integration.caption: Illustrative shapes, drawn from each vendor’s public naming. They were not generated from, or validated against, a vendor system; every real connector is built and checked against the client’s own system. Product names belong to their owners, and no partnership, certification or conformance is implied.

estate.scenario: A principal is preparing a signature residence for a small circle of buyers. Every viewing begins on the website, and each enquiry has to reach the right person, quickly and privately.
estate.c1: Heavy galleries and autoplaying media make the first impression slow exactly where the brand needs to feel effortless, above all on a phone.
estate.c2: Enquiries arrive as unstructured emails with no source, language or budget attached, so qualifying a buyer starts with a round of questions.
estate.c3: Availability and pricing live in several places, and a page that states something sales has not approved is a commercial and legal risk.
estate.s1: The arrival is a pre-rendered cinematic video, decoded by the device’s own hardware and loaded on demand, so the page opens instantly and the film starts only when it is seen.
estate.s2: Motion is composited on the GPU and limited to transform and opacity, and the layout is reserved up front, so nothing shifts while the page loads.
estate.s3: The enquiry is a four-step briefing that qualifies by design: investment band, project, timing and role arrive structured, with the visitor’s language and market attached.
estate.i1: Each enquiry is delivered to your CRM (Salesforce, HubSpot or Oracle are typical targets) as a structured record with its source, language and market, not as an email to be re-keyed.
estate.i2: Listing and availability can be read from your system of record, so the page never states something your sales team has not approved.
estate.i3: Every delivery is signed with HMAC-SHA256 and carries an idempotency key, so a retry is recognised and dropped by the receiver instead of creating a second lead. The secrets stay on the server.
estate.m1: Time from enquiry to the first personal reply
estate.m2: Share of enquiries that arrive complete and qualified

clinic.scenario: A private clinic wants a composed digital reception: physician profiles, a calm explanation of what it offers and a way for a patient to ask for an appointment, without a sales floor.
clinic.c1: The site has to feel as calm as the clinic. Pages that load slowly, jump while loading or shout with banners break trust in the first second.
clinic.c2: Requests arrive by phone or through open forms with no structure, so staff spend the day clarifying what a patient meant before they can help.
clinic.c3: Health communication is regulated: prices, discounts, galleries of results, patient testimonials and claims of superiority are not allowed, and a page that implies them is a liability.
clinic.s1: A quiet, pre-rendered reception film and restrained motion: nothing autoplays with sound, nothing moves unless the visitor chooses, and everything respects reduced-motion settings.
clinic.s2: Physician and service pages are plain, fast and exact. The patient starts the contact, and the page guides without alarming.
clinic.s3: A patient-initiated appointment request is structured so reception can answer it in one reply, and the site is designed so that no clinical information is collected on it.
clinic.i1: The request reaches your practice-management or CRM system (Oracle, SAP or Salesforce are typical targets) as a structured record, never as a message in a shared inbox.
clinic.i2: Only contact details and the request are processed: no diagnoses, images or records. Consent is explicit, the privacy notice names every processor, and a person reads every request.
clinic.i3: Every message is signed and verified, then sealed with AES-256 before it moves between systems, and access follows the principle of least privilege.
clinic.m1: Time from request to the first personal reply
clinic.m2: Share of requests that arrive complete
clinic.note: A concept render of a fictional clinic. Health communication rules apply (no prices, discounts, galleries of results or patient testimonials); applying them is the clinic’s responsibility, and every word is the clinic’s to approve.

law.scenario: A corporate law and advisory practice needs a presence that is restrained and exact: practice and partner pages, and a confidential way for a prospective client to make first contact.
law.c1: The first thing a client reads is discretion. A page that feels loud, slow or careless says something about the practice before a word of it is read.
law.c2: A confidential enquiry sent through an open form or a shared mailbox puts sensitive information where too many people can see it.
law.c3: Professional advertising rules restrict how a practice may describe itself and seek work, so every sentence on the page is a compliance decision.
law.s1: A dark, restrained interface whose motion is slow and optional. Structure comes first: practice, partner and enquiry pages that are fast, legible and exact.
law.s2: Nothing is published until a partner has approved the exact wording. The page structure makes every block of text a deliberate, reviewable decision.
law.s3: The confidential enquiry asks for the minimum: who is asking, how to reply and what kind of matter, in a form that never asks for the details of the matter itself.
law.i1: An enquiry reaches intake and conflict-check queues in the system your practice already runs (for example Oracle, SAP or Salesforce), not a shared mailbox.
law.i2: Zero trust at every boundary: each message is signed and verified, then sealed with AES-256-GCM before it moves between systems. Nothing is trusted on arrival.
law.i3: The page is built without cookies, analytics or advertising trackers, a person reads every request, and retention is limited to the period you define.
law.m1: Time from enquiry to the first partner-level reply
law.m2: Share of enquiries routed to the right practice group first time
law.note: A concept render of a fictional practice. Applying the advertising and communication rules of the profession is the practice’s responsibility; no client is solicited and every word is the practice’s to approve.

logistics.scenario: A logistics operator with sites in several countries runs orders, dock events and invoices across many systems. When one lane goes quiet, the others have to keep moving, and nobody should learn of it from a customer.
logistics.c1: Order, dock and invoice events pass through many systems. When one link stalls, events pile up silently and teams reconcile by hand, often after the customer has noticed.
logistics.c2: A single channel carries too much: one outage, one expired credential or one malformed message can stop a whole flow.
logistics.c3: Webhooks and integrations are trusted by default. An unsigned or replayed request can book the same event twice, or an event that never happened.
logistics.s1: A redundant queue architecture: when the primary channel goes quiet, events are accepted into a durable standby queue and drained in order once it recovers.
logistics.s2: Delivery is idempotent and bounded: every event has a key, retries are limited and always carry the same key, so a retry cannot book the same event twice.
logistics.s3: The operator’s interface is built to stay responsive under load: it renders from what it already has and updates in the background, so no screen waits for a busy back end.
logistics.i1: Order, dock and invoice events flow between the web layer and your ERP (SAP or Oracle) and CRM (Salesforce) through the redundant queue, so one failing lane never stops the others.
logistics.i2: Every webhook is signed and verified before anything trusts it, then sealed with AES-256-GCM in transit between systems.
logistics.i3: Bounded retries, dead-letter capture and alerts turn a silent failure into one that a person can see and fix.
logistics.m1: Time to recover after a channel interruption
logistics.m2: Events delivered once and in order, as a share of events sent
logistics.note: A concept render of a fictional operation. The capabilities described are the studio’s own statements about its method; no client result, uptime figure, SLA or certification is claimed.
